PMCs are increasingly used in aerospace and automotive applications due to their light weight and high strength-to-weight ratio relative to metals.
A major drawback of PMCs is their poor abrasion resistance, which restricts their use, especially at high temperatures.
The use of bond coats interleaved between a coating and a substrate with vastly different coefficients of thermal expansion is a common technique to improve coating adhesion or durability.

Prior collaborative research between NASA Glenn and AADC demonstrated that bond coats sandwiched between PMCs and high-quality plasma-sprayed, erosion-resistant coatings substantially improved the erosion resistance of PMCs.
The researchers used a non-contact technique called scanning optical interferometry to accurately determine the wear performance of erosion-coated PMCs while preserving the sample.

The erosion tests conducted at a velocity of 229 m/s with Arizona Road Dust particles at impingement angles of 20° and 90° showed that the coatings for PMCs remarkably reduced the erosion volume loss by a factor of approximately 10 compared to the uncoated samples.
Several erosion coatings for PMCs are currently being compared and down-selected for engine testing at Rolls Royce.
